ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Empirical Signatures of Choice-Induced Preference Change No ethics approval was required, as the study was based exclusively on the secondary analysis of previously published data.

In the original studies, participants completed modified versions of the free-choice paradigm: they first rated individual snack foods (images on a computer screen; either 100 or 60 snacks, depending on the experiment) in isolation, then chose between pairs constructed from the same set (each option appeared in exactly one pair), and finally rated the items again.

The pooled dataset included the subjective ratings that each participant provided for the overall value (V), the pleasure (P), and the nutrition (N) of each option, allowing us to calculate the difference in each type of rating (|dV|, |dP|, and |dN|, respectively) for each choice trial.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Choice-induced preference change refers to the tendency for value estimates to differ after a choice relative to before it.
Although this phenomenon is robust, the process that generates it remains debated.
In this work, we reanalyzed pooled data from two previous studies to identify empirical signatures that constrain candidate process accounts of choice-induced preference change.
We focused on three aspects of the choice process that are especially informative for theory: initial choice difficulty, deliberation dynamics, and the attribute structure of the options.
First, we reproduced the well-established finding that the spreading of alternatives is greater for more difficult choices.

Second, after controlling for initial choice difficulty, greater spreading was associated with shorter response times and higher confidence, indicating that these relationships are not reducible to initial value difference alone.

Third, we found that preference change depends not only on overall value difference but also on how the options differ in their attributes, with stronger effects for choices involving tradeoffs than for cases of simple dominance.

Together, these findings establish complementary empirical constraints on mechanistic accounts of choiceinduced preference change: an adequate process account must explain not only when preference change is greatest, but also how its magnitude relates to the dynamics and attribute structure of deliberation.
Traditional theories of value-based decision-making assume that the estimates of value we assign to choice options are fixed, at least within a given decision context.

However, many researchers have argued that preferences are constructed during a decision rather than simply retrieved from memory (or another source) and compared (Guo, 2016; Lichtenstein & Slovic, 2006; Payne et al., 1992; Slovic, 1995; Warren et al., 2011).
text.formatted: However, many researchers have argued that preferences are constructed during a decision rather than simply retrieved from memory (or another source) and compared <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Guo, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Lichtenstein & Slovic, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Payne et al., 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Slovic, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Warren et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: One consequence of contextdependent preference construction would be choice-induced preference change, for which there is substantial empirical evidence.
Value estimates differ systematically when people form them after versus before making choices between the options (see Enisman et al. (2021) for a metaanalysis).
text.formatted: Value estimates differ systematically when people form them after versus before making choices between the options (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Enisman et al. (2021)</ref> for a metaanalysis).

text.text: The key variable in that line of research is the spreading of alternatives (SoA): value estimates of the choice options spread apart during or after deliberation.

SoA is a robust phenomenon and is particularly high when choices are difficult (Liberman & Förster, 2006), when the certainty about option values is low (Lee & Coricelli, 2020; Lee & Daunizeau, 2020 , 2021) or when attribute disparity (i.e., the degree to which the choice involves a tradeoff between attributes) is high (Carpenter et al., 2016; Lee & Hare, 2023; Lee & Holyoak, 2021).

text.text: SoA also has systematic relationships with RT and choice confidence (Davydova et al., 2023; Lee & Holyoak, 2023).

text.text: Another body of literature in judgment and decision-making has extensively exposed related phenomena under the labels of information distortion (Carlson & Russo, 2001; Russo et al., 1996 Russo et al., , 2008) ) and coherence shifts (Holyoak & Simon, 1999; Simon et al., 2001 Simon et al., , 2004 Simon et al., , 2008)).

text.text: As with SoA, these phenomena involve reported preferences or evaluations that align more closely with the choice at the end of deliberation compared to the start.

Previous work has summarized several robust findings, including that distortion occurs for riskless and risky choices (DeKay et al., 2009); distortion can be substantial in magnitude (DeKay et al., 2011 (DeKay et al., , 2012)); and distortion Empirical Signatures of Choice-Induced Preference Change enhances the leading option while degrading the trailing option (DeKay, 2015).

text.text: Despite the extensive empirical exposition, however, the underlying process remains open to interpretation.
These traditions are relevant here because they offer alternative process-level interpretations of post-choice evaluation change.
Although choice-induced preference change has been studied for many decades and across disciplines, there is no consensus on a formal model to account for it.
Two broad classes of process account are especially relevant here.

One class of account explains SoA through dynamic value updating during deliberation, often within sequential-sampling or metacognitive-control frameworks (Bénon et al., 2024; Lee & Daunizeau, 2021; Lee & Pezzulo, 2026; Zylberberg et al., 2024).
text.formatted: One class of account explains SoA through dynamic value updating during deliberation, often within sequential-sampling or metacognitive-control frameworks <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Bénon et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Lee & Daunizeau, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Lee & Pezzulo, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Zylberberg et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Under this account, deliberation can refine initially uncertain value representations by recruiting additional processing.

Another class of account explains SoA through coherence-based reasoning, including parallel constraint satisfaction (PCS) models, in which representations mutually influence one another until the network reaches a coherent state (Holyoak & Simon, 1999; Simon et al., 2004; Simon & Read, 2025).

text.text: We focus on three features of the choice process that provide such constraints: initial choice difficulty, deliberation dynamics, and the attribute structure of the alternatives.
We treat these relationships as a joint empirical benchmark: accounting for any one signature is insufficient if the same process model cannot account for the others.
The primary goal of this study is not to adjudicate definitively between the different accounts, but rather to identify empirical signatures that any adequate account of SoA must reproduce.
To accomplish this, we re-examined multiple datasets from previously published studies (Lee & Hare, 2023; Lee & Holyoak, 2021).
text.formatted: To accomplish this, we re-examined multiple datasets from previously published studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Lee & Hare, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Lee & Holyoak, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: These datasets were chosen because they include pre-and post-choice value ratings, choices, and identifiable attribute ratings for each item.
They also include measures of RT and confidence, which provide additional information about the decision process.
In the analyses that follow, we focus on a concise set of findings that are especially relevant to these theoretical accounts.
First, we re-examine the established relationship between SoA and choice difficulty.
Second, we test whether the relationship between RT and SoA remains after controlling for difficulty.
Third, we test whether SoA depends not only on overall value differences between the options but also on the attribute structure of the choice.
Together, these analyses provide a focused set of empirical signatures to serve as benchmarks for process accounts of choice-induced preference change.

The datasets analyzed here have also been used to examine whether the contributions of individual attributes to value and choice vary dynamically across task phases and cognitive contexts [Lee & Pezzulo, JBDM].
text.formatted: The datasets analyzed here have also been used to examine whether the contributions of individual attributes to value and choice vary dynamically across task phases and cognitive contexts <ref type="bibr">[Lee & Pezzulo, JBDM]</ref>.

text.text: The present study addresses a distinct question.
Rather than asking how attribute weights change, we ask which trial-level empirical signatures of choiceinduced preference change must be jointly reproduced by candidate process models.
Accordingly, the present analyses focus on SoA as the outcome and examine its relationships with initial choice difficulty, deliberation time, confidence, and attribute disparity.

We reanalyzed pooled data from two previous studies (n = 473 total; n = 380 from Lee & Holyoak (2021) and n = 93 from Lee & Hare (2023)) to test how SoA relates to choice difficulty, response time, and attribute structure.
text.formatted: We reanalyzed pooled data from two previous studies (n = 473 total; n = 380 from <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Lee & Holyoak (2021)</ref> and n = 93 from <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Lee & Hare (2023)</ref>) to test how SoA relates to choice difficulty, response time, and attribute structure.

text.text: In the original studies, participants completed modified versions of the free-choice paradigm: they first rated individual snack foods (images on a computer screen; either 100 or 60 snacks, depending on the experiment) in isolation, then chose between pairs constructed from the same set (each option appeared in exactly one pair), and finally rated the items again.

The tasks differed from the standard free-choice paradigm in that participants here passively viewed all options in a pre-exposure phase, then provided ratings both for overall value and for individual attributes (pleasure and nutrition) for each option.
Additionally, participants reported confidence after each choice using a continuous slider scale.

We excluded 15 participants whose choices showed weak relationships with their reported ratings (operationalized as a slope coefficient of less than 1 in a participant-level logistic regression of choice on pre-choice value ratings) and the data for one participant was partially missing, leaving us with 457 participants (n = 365 from Lee & Holyoak (2021) and n = 92 from Lee & Hare (2023)) for analyses.

To better understand why attribute disparity predicts SoA, we tested how SoA might relate to the differences between the attribute estimates of choice pair options.

Specifically, we regressed SoA on dV (which has a well-documented relationship with SoA), dP, and dN, here each Empirical Signatures of Choice-Induced Preference Change calculated as the rating of the chosen option minus the rating of the rejected option (c-r).

We included the interaction of dP and dN as an additional regressor, to test for differences when one option scored more highly on both attributes versus when each option scored more highly on an attribute.
We found that dP and dN both have positive relationships with SoA (Figure 3).

The foregoing results provide a set of complementary constraints for candidate process accounts.

We focus on two prominent accounts of preference construction: the Metacognitive Control of Decisions (MCD) model of Lee and Daunizeau (2021) -which proposes that decision makers refine uncertain value estimates during deliberation through metacognitive control -and Parallel Constraint Satisfaction (PCS), in which representations change during deliberation as the decision system moves toward a coherent interpretation favoring one alternative.
text.formatted: We focus on two prominent accounts of preference construction: the Metacognitive Control of Decisions (MCD) model of <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Lee and Daunizeau (2021)</ref> -which proposes that decision makers refine uncertain value estimates during deliberation through metacognitive control -and Parallel Constraint Satisfaction (PCS), in which representations change during deliberation as the decision system moves toward a coherent interpretation favoring one alternative.

text.text: Any adequate account must explain why preference change increases with initial choice difficulty, while also explaining why, conditional on difficulty, greater change accompanies shorter response times and higher confidence.
It must additionally explain why preference change depends on the attribute structure of the alternatives beyond their overall value difference.
We therefore consider MCD and PCS in terms of their ability to account for this joint pattern.
One way to explain SoA is to assume that pre-choice value ratings are initially uncertain or incomplete and are refined during choice deliberation.

This idea is closely related to optimal sequential-sampling models (Fudenberg et al., 2020; Pezzulo et al., 2013; Tajima et al., 2016) and the metacognitive control of decisions (MCD) model (Bénon et al., 2024; Lee & Daunizeau, 2021), in which additional cognitive effort is recruited when existing value representations are insufficient to support a confident choice.
text.formatted: This idea is closely related to optimal sequential-sampling models <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Fudenberg et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Pezzulo et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Tajima et al., 2016)</ref> and the metacognitive control of decisions (MCD) model <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Bénon et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Lee & Daunizeau, 2021)</ref>, in which additional cognitive effort is recruited when existing value representations are insufficient to support a confident choice.

text.text: If initial value representations are imprecise, difficult choices will often motivate additional effort to refine them.

This refinement is thought to involve processing additional information, potentially including information about specific attributes, resulting in reported values that may differ after versus before the choice.
From this perspective, SoA would Empirical Signatures of Choice-Induced Preference Change not be a distortion but rather an outcome of task-relevant value updating.
In the present paper, we refer to this idea as the MCD account for brevity.
A different explanation comes from coherence-based reasoning models such as parallel constraint satisfaction (PCS; Holyoak & Simon (1999), Simon & Read (2025)).
text.formatted: A different explanation comes from coherence-based reasoning models such as parallel constraint satisfaction (PCS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Holyoak & Simon (1999)</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Simon & Read (2025)</ref>).

text.text: According to this account, deliberation is an interactive process in which representations of options, attributes, and possible conclusions mutually influence one another.
The decision process is conceptualized as a network in which nodes represent contextual features (e.g., options, attributes) and edges represent the relationships between features.
Across update iterations, as one option comes to dominate the other, features consistent with that option increase in activation and inconsistent features decrease in activation.
This results in a more coherent final state and, consequently, post-choice rating shifts akin to SoA.

Accounts of information distortion and coherence-based reasoning share the idea that evaluations become increasingly aligned with an emerging leader during deliberation; PCS provides a more explicit process account of how such shifts can arise.
In the present paper, we refer to this idea as the PCS account for brevity.
The two model classes described above operate in fundamentally different ways.
Under the MCD account, options compete based on noisy value signals that are incrementally refined through deliberation, leading to final value signals that may differ from the initial signals.
SoA thus reflects the choice-facilitating refinement of these value signals.

Under the PCS account, options compete based on network activity that evolves according to the pattern of connections Empirical Signatures of Choice-Induced Preference Change among representations, with coherence emerging from reciprocal constraints within the network.
SoA thus reflects the coherence-consistent restructuring of network activation.
How well can the two accounts explain the joint pattern identified here?

We consider three complementary constraints: the dependence of SoA on initial choice difficulty, the association of SoA with response time and confidence after controlling for difficulty, and the dependence of SoA on attribute structure beyond overall value difference.
Choice difficulty : SoA has a positive relationship with difficulty, which is a core feature of the phenomenon.
Both accounts predict greater SoA for more difficult choices.
Under the MCD account, difficult choices motivate further deliberation because preliminary value representations are insufficient to support commitment.
Under the PCS account, close competition between options generates greater tension in the network and may require more restructuring before a stable state is reached.
Thus, although the mechanisms differ, the basic difficulty effect alone provides little leverage for distinguishing the two accounts.
Deliberation dynamics : After controlling for initial choice difficulty, greater SoA was associated with shorter RT and higher confidence.

Under the MCD account, this pattern could arise if effective value refinement increases differentiation between the options and thereby facilitates confident commitment, whereas longer deliberation reflects unresolved uncertainty or ineffective processing.
Under the PCS account, stronger coherence formation could likewise increase differentiation between the alternatives while moving the system more rapidly toward a stable and confident choice.

Thus, either account must explain why greater preference change is associated not simply with more deliberation, but with faster and more confident resolution among choices of comparable initial difficulty.
Empirical Signatures of Choice-Induced Preference Change 3.
Attribute structure : SoA depends on the internal attribute structure of the choice beyond overall value difference, with greater preference change for choices involving stronger attribute tradeoffs.
Both accounts predict that SoA can increase when the options involve stronger attribute tradeoffs, even after controlling for overall difficulty.
Under the MCD account, such tradeoffs may require additional refinement of attribute estimates or of the weights by which attributes contribute to value.
Under the PCS account, configurations with strong tradeoffs create competing support within the network and may require more updating before a stable state is reached.
Considered individually, none of these signatures clearly distinguishes MCD from PCS.

Both accounts can plausibly accommodate greater SoA for difficult choices and choices involving stronger attribute tradeoffs, and both may accommodate the conditional associations of greater SoA with shorter response times and higher confidence.
The stronger theoretical constraint therefore lies in their conjunction.
An adequate mechanistic account should generate these relationships simultaneously from a common process rather than accommodate each independently through separate assumptions.
Determining whether formal implementations of MCD or PCS can reproduce this complete pattern would provide a more stringent basis for distinguishing the two accounts.
The present study sought to identify empirical regularities that mechanistic accounts of choice-induced preference change must account for jointly.

Across a large pooled dataset, SoA varied systematically with initial choice difficulty, deliberation time, confidence, and the attribute Empirical Signatures of Choice-Induced Preference Change structure of the choice.

Importantly, these relationships provide complementary rather than interchangeable constraints: a successful process account must explain both when preference change is greatest and how that change relates to the dynamics and structure of deliberation.
The present findings complement a separate analysis of these datasets examining dynamic changes in attribute weighting [Lee & Pezzulo, JBDM].
text.formatted: The present findings complement a separate analysis of these datasets examining dynamic changes in attribute weighting <ref type="bibr">[Lee & Pezzulo, JBDM]</ref>.

text.text: That work asks how the contributions of individual attributes to valuation and choice vary with task phase and cognitive context.

Here, by contrast, attribute structure is considered alongside difficulty and deliberation-related measures to identify behavioral constraints on mechanisms generating choice-induced preference change.
The observation that SoA is greater for more difficult decisions is consistent with decades of previous results.
However, this effect on its own is unable to distinguish between theoretical accounts.

Under a value refinement or metacognitive-control (MCD) account, difficult decisions motivate additional deliberation because preliminary value representations are insufficient to inform a confident choice.

Under a coherence-based reasoning or parallel constraint satisfaction (PCS) account, close competition between options creates greater tension in the network and may require more restructuring before a stable choice is reached.
Thus, both accounts can explain the basic difficulty effect, though they interpret the underlying process differently.
Accordingly, the difficulty effect is important but not strongly differentiating, because it is compatible with both value refinement and coherence-based accounts.
A related pattern -negative SoA for easy choices -should be interpreted cautiously.
Under the MCD account, easy decisions should require little refinement.
Under the PCS account, postchoice evaluations would be expected to move in a choice-consistent direction, but not necessarily by a large amount if the initial state is already close to coherence.

Thus, negative SoA for easy choices is difficult for both classes of account to explain in straightforward form and may partly Empirical Signatures of Choice-Induced Preference Change reflect regression-to-the-mean or scale-related effects.
Therefore, we cannot easily distinguish between them based solely on the data we currently have available.
The models might need to be extended with additional features to better explain this aspect of the data.
The relationship between SoA and RT is particularly informative because it has direct implications for how deliberation time should be interpreted.
Under MCD, one possibility is that longer deliberation would allow for more information processing and thus greater SoA.
However, effortful contemplation does not always lead to additional information processing (Lee, 2025).
text.formatted: However, effortful contemplation does not always lead to additional information processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Lee, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: If longer deliberation reflects unresolved conflict or inefficient effort rather than productive refinement, then the relationship would instead be negative.
Under PCS, longer RT may likewise correspond to more extensive coherence-building, but the relationship need not be monotonic because the network may sometimes stabilize quickly.
The present results are therefore important because they show that the RT-SoA relationship is not merely a byproduct of choice difficulty.
In the data we examined, greater SoA was associated with shorter RT and higher confidence, even when controlling for difficulty.

This pattern is consistent with the interpretation that greater SoA accompanies more effective deliberative resolution, whereas longer RT may reflect unresolved uncertainty rather than greater refinement.

However, this interpretation needs to be confirmed using supplementary experiments or additional (e.g., neural) measures that better distinguish in which cases additional time is really used to gather useful information.
The attribute-based results provide another useful constraint.
We found that SoA depended not only on the overall value difference between the chosen and rejected options, but also on the differences between those options in terms of pleasure and nutrition.
The more the chosen option surpassed the rejected option on a specific attribute, the more post-choice value ratings spread apart in favor of the chosen option.

At the same time, the negative interaction between pleasure Empirical Signatures of Choice-Induced Preference Change and nutrition indicated that this effect was reduced when one option scored more highly on both attributes.
In other words, SoA was especially related to choices involving strong attribute tradeoffs rather than simple dominance.

These results establish attribute structure as an additional constraint on mechanisms of preference change: models must explain not only why preference change increases with overall choice difficulty, but also why it varies systematically with the degree to which the alternatives involve competing attribute advantages.
Under the MCD account, such tradeoffs may motivate additional processing because the decision maker must refine how attributes contribute to value.
Under the PCS account, such tradeoffs create competing support within the network and may therefore require more restructuring before a coherent state is reached.
The attribute-based result is more informative than the basic difficulty effect, because it shows that SoA depends on the internal structure of the decision, not only on its overall difficulty.
The disparity-related effects are compatible with both of the accounts that we considered.
Taken together, the present results suggest that SoA is not merely a descriptive phenomenon and does not reflect a single uniform process.
It depends jointly on how difficult the decision is, how the options are structured in terms of their attributes, and how deliberation unfolds over time.
These findings are consistent with the idea that post-choice value ratings reflect dynamic processing rather than merely static value retrieval.
At the same time, the current data do not fully distinguish between value refinement and coherence-based reasoning.

More generally, the results indicate that any adequate account of SoA must explain not only why difficult choices produce greater preference change, but also why preference change depends on attribute structure and deliberation time in a systematic way.
Both of our candidate accounts can accommodate most of the observed patterns, but further testing with novel experiments could potentially discriminate between the two accounts.

text.text: The present results also contribute to the broader debate about value-based decisionmaking by suggesting that value estimates are not simply fixed quantities retrieved from memory.

Instead, they appear to be shaped by a constructive process in which attributes are considered, their relative contribution within the decision context is determined, and resulting value estimates may differ from initial appraisals.
This process is not yet fully captured by current computational models, but it is clearly richer and more dynamic than often assumed and therefore worthy of further investigation.

An adequate mechanistic account of choice-induced preference change must therefore explain not only why preferences diverge following difficult decisions, but also why the magnitude of that divergence covaries with deliberation time, confidence, and the attribute structure of the choice.
These joint empirical signatures provide a benchmark for developing and discriminating process models of preference construction.
Preferences change over the course of a decision, but the process underlying that change remains open to interpretation.

In this work, we showed that the spreading of alternatives (SoA) is greater for more difficult choices, that its relationship with response time remains after controlling for difficulty, and that it depends not only on overall value difference but also on the attribute structure of the decision problem.

Together, these findings indicate that choice-induced preference Empirical Signatures of Choice-Induced Preference Change change is tied to deliberation itself rather than to a static comparison of fixed value estimates.
More generally, any adequate account of SoA must explain why preference change depends jointly on choice difficulty, deliberation time, and attribute structure.
Any model, existing or novel, should look carefully at the relations between SoA and RT and at the fine-grained mechanisms of choice resolution.
Further progress will likely depend on a formal model comparison capable of determining value refinement, coherence-based reasoning, or other potential accounts explain this joint pattern.
